questions.title: Why convert
questions.text: Explain why sound must be converted from analogue to digital before it can be stored on a computer.

scheme.mark_scheme:

questions.title: Digital sound
questions.text: Explain how sound is represented digitally.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The amplitude of the wave is measured / sampled (1)
- at regular time intervals (sampling rate = samples per second) (1)
- each sample is stored as a binary number with a fixed number of bits (sample resolution) (1)
scheme.model_answer: The amplitude of the sound wave is measured at regular intervals; each measurement (sample) is rounded and stored as a binary number using a fixed number of bits.

questions.title: Reduce the size
questions.text: Describe **two** ways to reduce the size of a sound file, giving the drawback of each.

scheme.mark_scheme: Per way: method (1) + drawback (1). Lower sampling rate – high frequencies lost / lower quality; lower sample resolution – less accurate, more noise; mono – no stereo effect; lossy compression (MP3) – data permanently lost; shorter recording – less content.
scheme.model_answer: 1 Reduce the sampling rate — fewer samples so the sound is less accurate. 2 Record in mono — the left/right stereo effect is lost.

summary: How sound is digitised by sampling, what sampling rate, sample resolution and channels mean and how they affect quality and file size, why analogue sound must be converted to binary (ADC and DAC), and how to calculate the size of an audio file.

blocks.content: Sound is a **vibration** that travels through the air as a **wave**. A microphone turns these vibrations into a **continuously changing electrical voltage** — an **analogue signal**.
A signal that varies **continuously** and can take **any value** within a range — for example a real sound wave or the voltage from a microphone.
A signal made of **discrete (separate) values**, stored as **binary numbers** (0s and 1s).

items.title: Why sound must be converted to binary
items.content:
- A computer can **only store and process binary data** (0s and 1s); it cannot store a continuous wave.
- Digital sound can be **edited, copied, compressed and transmitted** without losing quality.
- It can be **stored** on storage devices and **streamed** over networks.

items.title: How it is converted
items.content:
- A **microphone** converts the sound wave into an analogue electrical signal.
- An **ADC (analogue-to-digital converter)**, usually on the **sound card**, measures the signal and converts it into **binary numbers**.
- To play the sound back, a **DAC (digital-to-analogue converter)** turns the binary values back into an analogue signal for the **speaker**.

blocks.content:
flowchart TB
  A[Sound wave] --> B[Microphone - analogue signal]
  B --> C[ADC - sampling and quantisation]
  C --> D[Binary data stored in a file]
  D --> E[DAC - binary to analogue]
  E --> F[Speaker - sound wave]
blocks.caption: From sound wave to file and back

blocks.content: Measuring the **amplitude (height) of the sound wave** at **regular time intervals** and storing each measurement as a **binary number**. Each measurement is called a **sample**.

blocks.caption: Sampling a sound wave (each | is one sample; the value is rounded to the nearest level)

blocks.content: The **number of samples taken per second**, measured in **hertz (Hz)**. CD-quality audio uses **44 100 Hz (44.1 kHz)** — 44 100 samples every second.
The **number of bits used to store each sample**. With *n* bits, **2ⁿ different amplitude levels** can be represented. CD audio uses **16 bits** (65 536 levels).

items.title: Channels
items.content:
- **Mono** — **1** channel; the same sound from every speaker.
- **Stereo** — **2** channels (left and right), so the file stores **twice** as many samples.
- Surround sound — 6 or more channels.

items.title: Quantisation
items.content:
- Each measured amplitude is **rounded** to the **nearest available level**.
- The difference between the real value and the stored value is the **quantisation error** — it is smaller when the sample resolution is higher.

theory.title: Effect on quality and file size

blocks.title: Sampling rate and sample resolution
rows: **More bits per sample** → more amplitude levels
The digital wave follows the original **more closely in time**; higher frequencies can be recorded
Each sample is **more accurate** (less rounding); **wider dynamic range**, less noise

blocks.content: Humans hear up to about **20 000 Hz**. To record a frequency accurately, you need **at least two samples per wave cycle** (the Nyquist rule), so the sampling rate must be more than **2 × 20 000 = 40 000 Hz**. 44 100 Hz is enough for all frequencies people can hear.

blocks.title: The trade-off
blocks.content: Better quality always means a **bigger file**: it needs more **storage**, more **bandwidth** to stream and **longer download** times. Choose settings that are **good enough** for the purpose — a voice message does not need CD quality.

theory.title: Calculating the size of an audio file

blocks.content:
**File size (bits) = sampling rate (Hz) × sample resolution (bits) × number of channels × duration (seconds)**

Then: **÷ 8 → bytes**, **÷ 1024 → KB**, **÷ 1024 → MB**. Always convert the duration to **seconds** first (3 minutes = 180 s).

blocks.title: Worked example 1 — 1 minute of CD-quality stereo
Worked example 3 — working backwards
blocks.content:
A **mono** recording uses **16-bit** samples, lasts **10 seconds** and has a file size of **441 000 bytes**. Find the sampling rate.
441 000 × 8 = 3 528 000 bits. 3 528 000 ÷ (16 × 1 × 10) = **22 050 Hz**.

blocks.title: Worked example 4 — a 3-minute song
blocks.content: 44 100 Hz, 16 bits, stereo, 3 min = 180 s: 44 100 × 16 × 2 × 180 = 254 016 000 bits = 31 752 000 bytes ≈ **30.28 MB**. That is why music is usually **compressed** (MP3 / AAC) to about 3 MB.

blocks.title: Ways to reduce the file size
rows: Smaller file; high frequencies are lost
Half the size; no left/right effect
About 10 × smaller; removes sounds people can hardly hear — cannot be restored
About 2 × smaller; the original can be restored exactly

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Explain how sound is represented digitally. [3]**
The amplitude of the sound wave is **measured (sampled)** at **regular intervals** (1); each sample is stored as a **binary number** using a fixed number of bits — the **sample resolution** (1); the number of samples per second is the **sampling rate** (1).

**Q: Explain why analogue sound must be converted before it can be stored on a computer. [2]**
A computer can only store and process **binary / digital** data (1); the sound wave is **continuous**, so an **ADC** must sample it and convert it to binary values (1).

**Q: Calculate the file size in MB of a 2-minute stereo recording with a sampling rate of 44.1 kHz and 16-bit resolution. [3]**
44 100 × 16 × 2 × 120 = 169 344 000 bits (1); ÷ 8 = 21 168 000 bytes (1); ÷ 1024 ÷ 1024 ≈ **20.19 MB** (1).

**Q: Describe the effect of increasing the sample resolution. [2]**
More amplitude levels, so each sample is **closer to the original** / better quality (1); the file size **increases** (1).

- Forgetting to **multiply by the number of channels** for stereo.
- Leaving the duration in **minutes**.
- Confusing **sampling rate** (samples per second) with **sample resolution** (bits per sample).
- Forgetting to **divide by 8** to get bytes.
- Saying a higher sampling rate makes the sound "louder" — it makes it **more accurate**.
